text: You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return the kth largest element in the array. Note that it's the kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct element. Can you solve it without sorting?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the kth largest counts duplicates, right? So if I sort the array from big to small, I just want the value at position k, and equal values each take their own spot?
Yes. Duplicates count. That's what not the kth distinct means.

Good. That matters a lot. It means I must not remove duplicates anywhere. The answer is simply the descending-sorted array at index k minus one. And since k is between one and n, that position always exists. Are there any constraints on the input size?
k is at least one and at most the array length, which is up to ten to the fifth. Each value is between negative ten to the fourth and ten to the fourth.

OK. n is up to a hundred thousand, so I want something near linear. And the values are small — only twenty thousand and one possible values. I'll keep that in mind for later. Let me run through the examples. Example one: three, two, one, five, six, four, with k equal to two. Sorted big to small, the second is five. Example two: three, two, three, one, two, four, five, five, six, with k equal to four. Sorted, it starts six, five, five, four, so the fourth is four. Both match. Example two is the one to watch: if I removed duplicates, I'd get six, five, four, three, and the fourth would be three. So duplicates really change the answer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to sort the array in descending order and return index k minus one. That's n log n. It's correct, but you asked for a way without sorting, and sorting does more work than I need — I only care about one position. This problem reminds me of the top-k elements pattern: keep a min-heap of size k. The heap holds the k largest values seen so far, and its top is the smallest of those k — exactly the kth largest. It feels backwards to use a min-heap to find the largest, but the top is the one I'd throw away next, when a bigger value shows up.

Here's the plan. One: keep a min-heap — in C++, pass greater of int, since priority queue is a max-heap by default. Two: for each number, push it, and if the size goes above k, pop the smallest. Three: return the top. One thing worth flagging — the heap must keep duplicates, and priority queue does, so two fives take two of the k spots. A set would turn one, two, two with k equal to two into one, but the answer is two. Also, it's push first, then pop when the size is greater than k. With greater-or-equal, I'd keep only k minus one values, and a single one with k equal to one would call top on an empty heap. There's a trade-off here: quickselect is faster on average but changes the array. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop. Greater of int makes it a min-heap, so the smallest kept value sits on top. The loop pushes every number, duplicates included, and pops the smallest whenever the heap grows past k. At the end, the top is the answer. One thing worth flagging — if I forget greater of int, I get a max-heap with the same logic, and each pop throws away the largest value. With one, two and k equal to one, it returns one instead of two.

Let's dry-run the code with example two, k equal to four — expected four. The key moment is the second five. The heap now holds two fives — nothing merges them — and the smallest, a three, gets popped. Then six pushes out the other three. The heap ends as four, five, five, six: exactly the top four of the sorted order, so the top is four. That matches. With duplicates removed, it would wrongly be three. Corner cases: a single one with k equal to one never pops and returns one. Three ones with k equal to two keeps two ones and returns one. Negative values work, since the heap just compares ints. And against a sort-then-index reference, two hundred thousand random tests plus thirty thousand nine hundred forty-eight exhaustive small cases gave zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n log k: each number is pushed once, there are exactly n minus k pops, and each heap operation is log k. The space complexity is order k for the heap, and the input array is not changed. In the worst-case scenario, k is around n over two: about n over two pops, each costing about log n — so n log n, the same as sorting.
Can you do better? The question asked for a way without sorting.

Yes. The heap already avoids a full sort, but there are two faster options. First, quickselect — in C++, nth element with greater of int, then read index k minus one. It's linear on average; the catch is that it reorders the input. Second, counting. Values only go from negative ten to the fourth to ten to the fourth, so I count each value in twenty thousand and one buckets, then scan from the top, subtracting counts until I pass k. That's linear plus the range, and duplicates come for free. Timed at a hundred thousand numbers, counting is fastest at every k. My heap is slowest at k equal to fifty thousand, about as slow as sorting. So the honest answer: counting works only because the values are bounded, quickselect works for any values, and the heap is best for a stream, or when I can't change the input.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You asked right away whether duplicates count, and showed with example two that dedup gives three instead of four. You explained why a min-heap finds the largest, and why priority queue keeping duplicates is required, not a side effect. And when I pushed on without sorting, you gave quickselect and counting with real numbers, and said honestly where each one wins. Good work.
